cards.name: The ad
cards.title: Free trading?
cards.situation: An app’s ad says: “Zero commission! Trading is free.” The app has hundreds of staff to pay. Is trading there really free?

options.feedback: Costs hit every trade, big or small. Even 10 shares with a $0.05 wider spread cost $0.50 a round trip, and that adds up.

options.text: No: they earn from my trades another way
options.feedback: Commission is only one fee. “Free” apps earn by selling your orders to market makers (payment for order flow) and through a wider spread, the bid–ask gap from Chapter 1.

options.text: Yes: zero commission means zero cost
options.feedback: It sounds like zero cost. But the app still earns on every buy and sell, through a wider spread or by selling your orders (payment for order flow).

cards.work: Spread $0.05 wider × 100 shares = $5 extra cost on every round trip.

cards.added: $0.06 × 100 = $6 example added · Visual: Two-row order book with a $0.06 spread on 100 shares
cards.title: Costs 1 and 2: commission and spread
cards.text: **[[commission|Commission]]**: a fee per trade or per share. Often zero now. **[[spread|Spread]]**: you met it in Chapter 1. You buy at the ask and sell at the bid, on every [[round-trip|round trip]] (one buy plus one sell). A $0.06 spread on 100 shares = $6 a round trip, commission or not.

cards.added: Numbers $10.00 / $10.08 added (p.15 defines slippage) · Visual: Slippage receipt drawn after the tap: expected $10.00, got $10.08, 100 shares = $8
cards.title: Cost 3: slippage
cards.text: News breaks. You tap Buy at $10.00 with a market order. Prices are jumping, and you’re filled at $10.08. That 8-cent gap between the price you expected and the price you got is **[[slippage|slippage]]**. On 100 shares: $8. It’s biggest in fast markets and with market orders, and now and then it goes your way.

cards.added: $1 a night × 90 nights = $90 example added (p.15 defines swaps) · Visual: Night counter drawn at night 90: $1 a night fills a $90 jar
cards.title: Cost 4: swap
cards.text: Hold a leveraged position overnight and you pay interest: **overnight financing**, a **[[swap|swap]]** on forex and CFDs or **margin interest** on US stocks. A swap is charged on the full position, not just your deposit. Say it’s $1 a night. One night is nothing. Three months (90 nights) is $90, eaten from your gains even if the price never moves.

cards.added: Two-broker comparison (the old Call, smaller numbers): A = $0.06 × 100 × 10 = $60; B = $1 × 2 × 10 + $0.01 × 100 × 10 = $30 · Visual: Two-column broker price list for the Try it
cards.name: Compare the bills
cards.title: Which broker is cheaper?
cards.q: You buy and sell 100 shares 10 times a month. Which broker costs less per month?

options.text: Broker A: zero commission is cheapest
options.feedback: Zero commission looks cheapest. But A’s spread is much wider, and you pay it on every share of every trade.
The costs come in different forms, but they don’t match. Add each broker’s commission and spread before comparing.
Broker B charges a commission, but its spread is so narrow that its total cost is half of A’s.
That counts only B’s commission. B has a spread too; add it in.

cards.work: A: $0.06 spread × 100 shares × 10 trips = $60 cost. B: $1 × 2 trades × 10 trips = $20 commission + $0.01 × 100 × 10 = $10 spread = $30 cost.

cards.title: The overnight bill
cards.q: You hold a $10,000 leveraged position for 30 nights. The swap is $1 a night. What does holding it cost?

options.feedback: Swap is charged every night you hold, even if the price never moves.
Swap is charged for every night you hold, whatever the price does. Thirty nights means thirty charges.
That’s one night. You held it for 30, and the swap is charged every night.
Check the decimal point. It’s $1 a night, for 30 nights, not $10 a night.

cards.headline: You can spot the hidden costs on any trade.
lines: Four costs: commission, spread, slippage, swap (overnight financing).
“Zero commission” can still cost more: check the spread.
Holding leverage overnight costs swap (or margin interest) every night.
